questions.q: What does ordinary least squares choose?
options: The line that passes through the most data points exactly
The line with the largest slope
The intercept and slope that minimize the sum of squared residuals
The line that ignores outliers completely
questions.explain: OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals, the gaps between actual values and predictions. It does not require passing through points and is actually sensitive to outliers.

options: The difference between the actual value and the model's prediction
The slope of the fitted line
The number of features in the model
The share of variation the model explains
questions.explain: A residual is actual minus predicted for one data point. The share of variation explained is R-squared.

questions.q: In scikit-learn, why do we call sqft.reshape(-1, 1) before fitting with one feature?
options: To convert the values to strings
To scale the values between 0 and 1
To remove outliers
Because X must be two-dimensional, with shape (rows, features)
questions.explain: scikit-learn estimators expect X as a 2D array of shape (n_samples, n_features), even when there is only one feature.

questions.q: In the lesson, the fitted slope was 119.5 while the data was built with a slope of 120. Why isn't it exactly 120?
options: The model has a bug
Random noise was added to prices, so the fit recovers the truth only approximately
R-squared was too low
LinearRegression always rounds slopes
questions.explain: Normally distributed noise was added to each price, so the best-fit line from 60 noisy points lands close to, but not exactly on, the built-in relationship.

questions.q: The lesson reports R-squared of 0.949 from model.score(X, price) on the training data. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The model will be 94.9% accurate on any new house
The line explains about 95% of the variation in training prices, but test data is needed to judge generalization
The model is guaranteed not to overfit
94.9% of houses are predicted exactly
questions.explain: R-squared is the share of variation explained. Computed on training data it does not tell you how well the model generalizes; a held-out test set does.
